name: Gold thread lift

lead: Gold thread implantation places very fine strands of gold under the skin, historically in parts of Asia, aiming for tighter skin, fewer wrinkles or a lifting effect on the face. Looksmaxxing discussion of it is sparse.

Proponents describe the threads as stimulating the skin or supporting tissue, and a histopathology study examined skin that had gold threads implanted for facial rejuvenation. One series of 78 patients in Archives of Plastic Surgery looked at gold thread implantation for crow's feet. Most other literature is case reports of threads found on X-rays or CT scans years after treatment.

paras: Threads are inserted under the skin by a practitioner, in cosmetic clinics or acupuncture-style settings. It is sometimes mentioned as an alternative to thread lifts. Gold threads are permanent, so they stay in place after the visible effect has been and gone.

Case reports describe threads migrating, recurrent cellulitis, and incidental findings on imaging that can be mistaken for other conditions or obscure dental imaging. In one fatal case report, gold threads were found at autopsy alongside electroacupuncture injuries; the report attributed the death to pneumothoraces from electroacupuncture, not the threads. Because the threads are permanent, they cannot simply be left to dissolve.

angle.text: Gold threads placed under the skin are promoted for smoother, tighter skin and fewer wrinkles through a skin reaction around the threads. A small series of 78 patients studied it for crow's feet, and case reports describe threads staying in place for years.

lead: Gold thread lift, also called gold thread implantation or gold thread therapy, is a cosmetic procedure in which very fine gold strands are placed just beneath the skin. People seek it as a minimally invasive way to soften wrinkles, especially around the eyes, and to give the skin a firmer, 'lifted' look without surgery or repeated injections. Closely related gold-thread practices in some Asian clinics are offered for pain relief and are described as a form of acupuncture. [1][2][3]

The idea is that the threads stay in place permanently and act as a scaffold the body responds to. The authors of the best-known cosmetic series describe a proposed sequence in which a capsule forms around each thread, collagen builds up, new small blood vessels form and mast cells increase, which they present as the rationale for the treatment rather than something they demonstrated. [2] The appearance chain is therefore thread placed, tissue reaction, firmer and smoother skin.

The clinical literature is small. A single-arm 2012 Korean study followed 78 patients with crow's feet for 12 weeks [1][2], and a 2015 histopathology study described how implanted threads look in skin tissue [4]. Most other publications are case reports and letters in radiology, dentistry, dermatology and forensic medicine, in which gold threads placed years earlier turn up on imaging [5][6][7][8][9][10]. The procedure is mentioned only occasionally in looksmaxxing discussion, usually as an alternative to absorbable thread lifts.

paras: In published case reports, patients describe having gold threads implanted for facial rejuvenation or to relieve neck, back or joint pain, often through clinics offering acupuncture-style treatment. [5][11][12] Gold is radiopaque, so retained threads can appear on X-ray, CT and dental panoramic images. [5][6][10]

In the 2012 crow's feet series, six threads about 4 cm long and 0.1 mm thick were placed under the skin at roughly half-centimetre intervals in each patient under local anaesthesia, and the threads were braided with absorbable polyglycolic acid. [2] The authors described gold as chemically stable and non-allergenic and noted its existing use in dental work and in gold weights for the eyelid. [2]

A report on cellulitis in a patient with gold threads describes the practice in a different setting: gold thread acupuncture is used in several Asian countries, mainly for pain such as headache and osteoarthritis, and the implanted threads are thought by practitioners to provide continuous stimulation. The authors of that report note that little scientific evidence addresses its efficacy or safety. [3]

Proponents and the authors of the cosmetic series suggest that subdermal gold threads provoke a capsule with collagen formation, promote angiogenesis and increase mast cell numbers over time, which would thicken and firm the dermis. [2] A histopathologic and electron-microscopy study of skin that had received threads for facial rejuvenation described the tissue features around the implants. [4] Neither study measured long-term lifting of sagging tissue; the 2012 study framed the mechanism as the rationale for testing, not a demonstrated result. [2]

A 2012 study in Archives of Plastic Surgery evaluated gold thread implantation for periorbital wrinkles in 78 consecutive patients (69 women and 9 men, aged 31 to 59) with mild to severe crow's feet. It had no control group and followed patients at 1, 4 and 12 weeks. [1][2]

On the Wrinkle Severity Rating Scale, scored from photographs by two plastic surgeons, the mean score fell from 3.21 at baseline to 2.41 at 12 weeks, and about 80 percent of patients improved by more than one point. Patients' own global assessment on a visual analog scale fell from about 70 to about 28. The only complications reported were a foreign-body sensation in the eye in 2.63 percent and eye pain in 1.32 percent, both of which resolved on their own. [2]

The authors listed the small sample, lack of a control group and short follow-up as limitations, said it was unclear whether the effect outlasts non-surgical alternatives, and called for larger controlled studies. [2] A histopathologic and ultrastructural study described the features of threads implanted in skin for facial rejuvenation. [4] No randomized controlled trials have been identified.

A case report describes a 75-year-old woman with recurrent cellulitis of the lower leg associated with migratory gold threads; threads implanted in her back about ten years earlier were hypothesised to have travelled to the leg, and the authors suggested tissue damage made it more prone to infection. She improved on antibiotics and a short steroid course, but the threads were not removed and she was told infection could recur. [11][3] The authors also cite local reactions reported with gold thread acupuncture, including bleeding, haematoma, inflammation and foreign-body granuloma, and note that lack of regulation can lead to contamination. [3]
Reports describe threads in the periorbital region, throughout the whole body, and around the sacroiliac joints in a patient seeking relief for ankylosing spondylitis. [8][7][12]

Radiology and dental reports note that worm-like radiopaque lines from gold threads can be misread as parasites, fractures or ligature wires, and can reduce the diagnostic quality of dental panoramic images. [6][10][13][9][5]

A forensic case report described a man in his 60s who died after electroacupuncture; imaging showed bilateral pneumothoraces and numerous subcutaneous gold threads. The authors attributed the pneumothoraces to needles penetrating the lung, not to the threads. [14]

Gold thread lift is rarely discussed in looksmaxxing communities. When it comes up, it is grouped with other thread-based procedures that aim to tighten skin without surgery, such as absorbable thread lifts. Its permanence is the point of contrast: unlike absorbable threads, gold threads are intended to remain, which is also why they show up on imaging years later. [2][5][10]

Related options for periorbital wrinkles named in the 2012 study's background include botulinum toxin, lasers, chemical peels and retinoids, which the authors described as needing repeat treatment or carrying cost, complication or consistency limits. [2]

timeline.event: Gold thread use in dermatology is described as having been introduced in France about 30 years before the 2012 study. [2]
Archives of Plastic Surgery publishes a 78-patient single-arm study of gold threads for crow's feet. [1]
A histopathologic and ultrastructural study of gold threads implanted for facial rejuvenation is published. [4]
A radiology report describes numerous linear metallic densities identified as gold threads. [9]
A case report describes multitudinous gold threads throughout the whole body. [7]
Reports describe recurrent cellulitis with migratory gold threads and a dental panoramic image degraded by cosmetic gold threads. [11][10]
Case reports describe gold threads on a chest radiograph, on cervical spine imaging, around the sacroiliac joints, and in a fatal electroacupuncture case. [6][5][12][14]
Orbit publishes a report on periorbital golden threads. [8]
